title: Distributed File System and Shared Memory - GeeksforGeeks
content:
A Distributed File System (DFS) lets multiple clients access and share files stored across different physical machines as if they were on a local disk, while Distributed Shared Memory (DSM) extends that illusion of a single shared address space across networked machines.

  • Presents files spread across multiple servers under a single, location-transparent namespace.
  • Handles replication and caching to improve performance and availability.
  • Uses fault-tolerance mechanisms like atomic commit protocols to keep data consistent despite failures.
  • DSM lets processes on separate machines share data through a common memory abstraction instead of explicit message passing.
  • Consistency models define how up-to-date a read is guaranteed to be after a write elsewhere in the system.

DFS Basics

  • Characteristics of File system
  • Network file system architecture
  • Andrew file system
  • Design Principles of DFS

File Service Architecture and Models

The components that define how a DFS presents, locates, and manages files for clients. They can be broadly categorized into:

File Service Architecture

File Service Architecture describes how the directory service, flat file service, and client module together provide file access over a network.

File Models

File Models define how a file is structured and interpreted as an unstructured byte stream, a record sequence, or a tree.

File-Accessing Models

File-Accessing Models describe how clients read and write remote files:

  • Remote service model: requests are sent to the server for every access.
  • Data-caching model: file data is cached locally to reduce network traffic.

File-Sharing Semantics

File-Sharing Semantics define what guarantees a client gets when multiple processes access the same file concurrently — Unix semantics, session semantics, and transaction semantics.

File-Caching Schemes

File-Caching Schemes determine where cached file data lives (client memory, client disk, or server) and how cache consistency is maintained.

Replication and Fault Tolerance

  • Replication: Storing multiple copies of a file across servers to improve availability and fault tolerance.
  • Atomic commit protocol: Ensures a distributed transaction either commits on all participating servers or none at all.

Distributed Shared Memory (DSM)

Distributed shared memory provides processes on different machines a shared logical address space, avoiding explicit message-passing code and simplifying parallel programming.

  • Architecture of Distributed shared memory: How DSM is layered over the underlying network and memory management units.
  • Uniform Memory Access (UMA) vs Non-uniform Memory Access (NUMA): UMA gives every processor equal-latency access to all memory; NUMA gives faster access to local memory over remote memory.
  • Design and implementation issue of distributed shared memory: Covers granularity, replacement strategy, and thrashing control.
  • Algorithm for implementing DSM: Includes central-server, migration, read-replication, and full-replication algorithms.

Consistency and Performance

  • Consistency models: Define the rules (strict, sequential, causal, weak, etc.) governing when writes become visible to other processes.
  • Thrashing in Distributed shared memory: Occurs when data is moved between nodes repeatedly, degrading performance instead of improving it.
